notes.use_when: A request names the viola d'amore, or asks for a Baroque/operatic obbligato with a ringing, sympathetic-string halo.
notes.summary: Never a regular orchestral member; a solo/obbligato colour. Seven bowed strings tuned to D major (A2 D3 A3 D4 F#4 A4 D5 = 45 50 57 62 66 69 74; lowest uncertain) over seven sympathetic strings tuned in unison. Range ≈ A2–A6 (45–93). Chords, arpeggios and natural harmonics in D major/minor are easy, and that ringing is the point. Without a dedicated library, fake it with a solo viola plus a resonance layer (inferred).

notes.title: Viola positions, chords, harmonics and pizzicato (playability checks)
notes.use_when: Checking whether a generated viola line, chord, harmonic, pizz or high passage is playable before writing it to MIDI or exporting parts.
notes.summary: Viola fingering equals the violin's a fifth lower but with wider spacing. Keep fast or long passages at or below 3rd position (top ≈ G5, 79) and allow no stretch beyond a P4 inside one hand position. Prefer 3-note, open-spaced chords on open strings. Harmonics speak easily: stopped notes ≤ D5 give touch-4th harmonics ≤ D7 (98). Pizz is rounder than the violin's but hard and wooden above ≈ E5 (76).

notes.title: Viola
notes.use_when: Writing, checking or voicing a viola part (inner voice, filler, light bass, doubling or melody) in MIDI.
notes.summary: Viola sounds as written (alto clef), C3 up to E6 (48–88), practical 48–81 and most comfortable ≤ G5 (79). Too small for its pitch, it sounds dark and veiled. The C string (48–55) is menacing or delicate, G/D (55–69) are the gentle accompaniment strings, and the A string (69+) is nasal and penetrating. It is the busiest inner voice: filler, doubling of violins or cellos, a light bass, singing melody. Write double notes as divisi. Technique limits: [[viola-technique-limits]].

notes.title: Violin positions, leaps, chords and harmonics (playability checks)
notes.use_when: Checking whether a generated violin line, leap, chord, arpeggio, glissando or harmonic is playable (section or solo) before writing it to MIDI.
notes.summary: Judge difficulty by strings and shifts, not interval size; first position (55–83) is the safest zone. A slurred leap needs its two notes on the same or adjacent strings. Chords use adjacent strings, ≤ P8 between neighbours in one position, open strings help, and 3–4-note chords roll bottom-up with only the top 1–2 held. Touch-a-4th harmonics sound +24; natural harmonics stop at the 5th partial.

notes.title: Violin (Vln I / Vln II)
notes.use_when: Writing, checking or voicing a violin I / violin II part (section or solo) in MIDI: range, string colour, Vln I/II roles, solos and doublings.
notes.summary: Violin sounds as written; sections G3–E7 (55–100), most secure 55–88, Classical pastiche ≤ A6 (93), solo to ≈ B7 (107). Colour follows the string, not the octave: E (76+) brightest and strongest, G (55–72) dark and second in power, D (62–74) weakest, A (69–81) strong low and softer high. Vln I carries the themes; Vln II doubles it or accompanies. Positions, leaps, chords and harmonics are in [[violin-technique-limits]].

notes.title: Woodwind articulation, tonguing and extended techniques
notes.use_when: Deciding how woodwind notes are attacked and connected (slurs, staccato, double/triple tonguing, fp envelopes) or writing flutter-tongue, glissando, key clicks, multiphonics and other effects.
notes.summary: Unslurred wind notes are each tongued (separate attacks); a slur is one breath with only its first note tongued. Double/triple tonguing is idiomatic on flute and an emergency on reeds; fp and sf>p<f envelopes suit wind chords. Flutter-tongue is easy on flutes, clarinets and saxes, poor on oboe and bassoon; glissando only upward on clarinet and sax; other effects are soft, rare and must be described in words.

notes.title: Woodwind basics
notes.use_when: Before writing for any woodwind, to pick the instrument and register, check transposition and dynamics by register, plan breaths and choose the section size for an era.
notes.summary: Four families (flutes, oboes, clarinets, bassoons; saxes apart) differ by reed, bore and overblowing (octave, clarinet a 12th). Pick a woodwind's register for colour and carrying power: flutes are weak low and grow upward, oboe and bassoon never pp in their lowest fifth, only the clarinet has full dynamics everywhere; extremes are hard, the top more than the bottom. Every line must breathe; modern default section = by threes.

notes.title: Separation vs fusion of lines
notes.style_scope: universal (method from film scoring, backed by Adler 2002 and Piston 1955)
notes.use_when: Two or more simultaneous lines must be heard as different things (melody vs countermelody, theme vs ostinato, canon entries), or several instruments must fuse into one gesture.
notes.summary: Lines separate when they differ in the main parameters (rhythm/articulation, register, timbre) and fuse when they share them. Dynamics and contour are secondary, prior exposure and best-register placement help, and pan and depth are a mix-stage extra. To make lines independent, change at least one main parameter, ideally two. To fuse, match rhythm, register and colour, and beware of accidental fusion: a new entry a step from another instrument's last note, or close lines doubled in octaves.

notes.title: Orchestra line-ups by era (Baroque to film)
notes.style_scope: period practice (Renaissance to modern film); the modern default stays in the main note
notes.use_when: Choosing the forces for a piece in a named period or composer's manner (Baroque, Haydn/Mozart, Beethoven, Wagner, Mahler, film), or checking that a template has no anachronistic instruments.
notes.summary: Line-ups grow from a string core with variable winds (Baroque) to the Classical a2 orchestra (2 fl/ob/cl/bsn, 2 hn, 2 tpt, timpani, no trombones in symphonies), the Romantic a3 with auxiliaries and trombones, the late-Romantic large orchestra (strings 18-16-14-12-10, 8 horns) and the modern standard (4 hn, 3 tpt, 3 trb, tuba). Film adds huge brass. Track order follows score order: woods, horns, trumpets, trombones, tuba, timpani, percussion, harp/keys, strings.

notes.title: Orchestra sizes, section balance and sample patch size
notes.style_scope: universal (section table = modern recording practice; period line-ups in the -by-era note)
aliases: dos trompas igual a una trompeta
notes.use_when: Choosing the line-up of a piece or cue, deciding how many players a string part stands for, weighing sections against each other, or picking solo / chamber / full-section sample patches.
notes.summary: String sections are sized for loudness AND type of sound and shrink from Vln I to Cb (modern full section 16/14/12/10/8, Adler up to 18/16/14/12/10). Balance weights at forte: 1 trumpet ≈ 1 trombone ≈ 2 horns, woodwinds weakest; one woodwind on a string line is absorbed, two tint it. Solo patch = 1–3 players, chamber ≈ 4–8, full section = 9+; never fake a section with stacked solo patches. Period line-ups: [[orchestra-sizes-and-section-balance-by-era]].

notes.title: Pointillism and Klangfarbenmelodie (tone-colour melody)
notes.style_scope: Second Viennese School (1909–1940s) and later modernist writing; ALLOWED sparingly as a colour in tonal and film music
notes.use_when: Writing a line where almost every note changes instrument (pointillist, Webern-like, fragmented, glassy or modernist colour), or colouring a repeated note across several instruments.
notes.summary: A Klangfarbenmelodie spreads one continuous phrase over many instruments, nearly one note each; pointillism adds octave displacements and a separate dynamic per note. It only works if every duration, articulation and dynamic is exact, because the listener rebuilds the line from isolated points. Era-bound to Webern and the Second Viennese School; in tonal or film music use it briefly, with solo patches, for a fragmented or crystalline colour.

notes.title: Orchestral colour effects (two-colour sforzando, subito piano, dovetailing, note colouring)
aliases: usos de la orquesta para efectos especiales
notes.use_when: Making an orchestral accent, a sudden drop from ff to p, a seamless relay of a figure between sections, a held note that changes colour, or marking which line is principal in a dense texture.
notes.summary: Orchestral effects come from combining sections, not from one track's CC. An sf is two colours on one attack (a short pizz, trumpet or oboe note over a held note); a forte-subito-piano is a soft group entering under a loud one that then stops; a seamless relay shares one note between outgoing and incoming instruments; a held note can be coloured by passing it between instruments at one soft dynamic. In dense textures mark the principal line one dynamic level above the rest.

notes.title: Translating piano idioms into the orchestra (pedal, decay, figures, recolouring)
notes.style_scope: universal (devices from Adler's piano-to-orchestra models — Ravel, Bizet, Brahms, Dvořák, Mussorgsky/Ravel, Schumann, Mozart)
notes.use_when: Converting a specific piano figure (sustain pedal, fermata, arpeggiated or repeated chords, octaves, ostinato, runs, tremolo, ornaments) into orchestral parts, or recolouring the repeats of a piano piece.
notes.summary: Each piano device has an orchestral equivalent. Pedal resonance becomes written held notes (horns, low clarinet + Cb pizz.), a decaying fermata a measured hold, hand-span arpeggios block chords, repeated chords string repeated notes, octaves a clarinet choir or Vln I + Vc in octaves. Ostinati go to one mid-string section, runs relay low to high. Soft passages sit in controllable registers, and every repeat changes at least one layer's family.

notes.title: Other transcriptions (chamber group to orchestra, and scoring for whatever ensemble is available)
notes.style_scope: universal (Stravinsky/Pulcinella and Schoenberg/Brahms models; Adler's school-ensemble workflow)
notes.use_when: Orchestrating a trio sonata, string quartet or piano quartet, or arranging any piece for a given or incomplete instrument set (a library that lacks instruments, a school or community group).
notes.summary: For a chamber source, keep the harmony (take it from the figured bass, not a later editor), set concertino against ripieno, and let winds double outer voices only in tutti phrases, then drop out so a solo pair sounds fresh. For an odd ensemble, reduce to piano, label passages tutti/mezzo tutti/soli/solo, and substitute missing soloists by a similar instrument, then a two-instrument blend, then range and dynamic fit. Reinforce the bass and keep percussion sparse.

notes.title: Orchestrating from a piano sketch or MIDI reduction (step by step)
notes.style_scope: universal (UNIR method + Adler ch.17 keyboard-to-orchestra principles; also fits original sketches)
notes.use_when: Turning a piano piece, a piano-roll sketch, a lead sheet or a one-track MIDI reduction into an orchestral MIDI arrangement in REAPER.
notes.summary: Decide first whether it is a transcription (complete piece) or an arrangement (melody only, so write a full short score first). Rank the layers (melody, bass, filler, motor), keep the register layout, translate piano idioms instead of imitating them, write crescendi by adding instruments, change colour only at phrase boundaries, and recolour repeats. Never change the harmony or form of an existing piece.

notes.title: Transcription, band and layout errors (extra checks)
notes.use_when: Validating an orchestration made from a piano, chamber or band source, a band arrangement, or a new orchestral template, after the main error checklist.
notes.summary: Extra checks for transcriptions: piano leftovers (CC64, strummed onsets, imitated tremolos, unmeasured fermatas), changed harmony or untagged additions, a principal voice that does not lead, band masses mapped 1:1, missing-instrument lines dropped, unplanned substitutes, overused percussion and amateur extremes. Layout checks: track order, family folders, doubling players playing two instruments at once.

notes.title: Common orchestration errors (final checklist)
notes.use_when: Validating any generated orchestral MIDI before handing it to the user, or diagnosing why a mock-up sounds unclear, thin or unbalanced.
notes.summary: Check two classes of error. Instrumental errors belong to one track: out of range, unplayable leaps or tremolos, extreme notes at the wrong dynamic, no breaths, octave doublings past a range. Discursive errors belong to the ensemble: cut lines, colour changes mid-phrase, a covered melody, forte arrivals with few instruments, unison doublings that cancel, repeats never recoloured, sections that never rest. Run every check vertically and horizontally; transcriptions and band work add the checks in the transcription note.

notes.title: Percussion for climaxes, openings and march or folk colour
notes.style_scope: universal (Adler's repertoire models; Turkish and Spanish kits era-tagged)
notes.use_when: Using percussion to build, sustain or crown a climax, to open a piece or movement, to end with drums alone, or to evoke a march, alla turca or Spanish/Mediterranean colour.
notes.summary: Build a climax by stages, each adding a percussion colour (timpani pp pedal ostinato → single strokes → main motif → snare → cymbals at the peak), or reserve the timpani and bring them in late (sparse hits → roll → doubling the brass rhythm on tonic/dominant → roll into the last chord). Openings can be a soft timpani motif, a cymbal crash after a quiet movement or a timpani roll into an ostinato. Turkish colour = bass drum, cymbals, triangle, no timpani.

notes.title: Writing for the percussion section (players, order, jobs, colour)
notes.style_scope: universal (Adler 2002 / Piston 1955 orchestral practice; period colour kits era-tagged)
aliases: distribución de la percusión en la partitura
notes.use_when: Deciding whether, where and how percussion enters a cue, how many players it needs, how to order its tracks, and how to combine it with piano, celesta, harp or mallets.
notes.summary: Every percussion entry needs a job (march/folk colour, accent reinforcement, climax, dramatic opening, colouring notes) or it goes; fewer is better, and ff timpani + bass drum masks everything. Plan 3–4 players plus timpanist and keyboard player, ≤ 2 instruments per player at once, rolls need both hands, switches need time. To reinforce, double only the accents of another section on the same rhythm with one dry colour.

notes.title: Score order, parts and cues (track order, family folders, doublings, substitutes)
notes.style_scope: universal (modern concert practice; band order differs, see wind-band)
notes.use_when: Ordering and grouping tracks for an orchestral template, placing extra instruments (saxes, euphonium, Wagner tubas, alto flute), planning player doublings (muta in), exporting a condensed score or piano reduction, or covering a missing instrument with a cue.
notes.summary: Score order = track order. Woodwinds (picc, fl, ob, Eng hn, small cl, cl, bass cl, bsn, cbsn), then brass (hn, tpt, trb, tuba), timpani and percussion, harp, keyboards, then strings (Vln I, Vln II, Va, Vc, Cb), with one folder per family. Extras go inside their family. One track per player-part, each with its own dynamics. A condensed score is 3–4 concert-pitch staves; a piano reduction drops octave doublings. Cue important lines so a missing player or patch never loses them.

notes.title: Sound planes (foreground, middleground, background) and how to stage them
notes.style_scope: universal (orchestral practice; mix numbers = mock-up practice, inferred)
notes.use_when: Making a melody stand in front of its accompaniment, deciding which line is foreground, middleground or background, handing the foreground between sections, or translating planes into level, depth and pan in REAPER.
notes.summary: Planes are built in the orchestration before the mix. Give the foreground its best register and a colour that contrasts with the background; bring a new foreground in with a new colour at its phrase start (upbeat included) or after a silence; turn the outgoing section into background a bar early; keep a colour in reserve. The background must never cover the melody: thin layers, staggered rests, light articulation. Only then use CC levels, reverb depth and pan to confirm the planes.

notes.title: Stage seating to pan and depth map
notes.style_scope: universal (seating = orchestral practice; pan values = mock-up practice)
notes.use_when: Setting pan and depth for orchestral tracks in REAPER, or deciding whether a library's baked-in hall position should be kept.
notes.summary: Pan follows the audience's view of the stage. Strings sit in front from left to right, woodwinds in the centre, horns and brass behind, and percussion at the back. Libraries recorded in place (Spitfire/Albion) already contain that position, so leave them near centre. Dry libraries get the pan values and depth sends from the table. Choose one seating (modern or antiphonal) for the whole cue. Musical planes (foreground/background) come from the orchestration first: [[stage-seating-pan-depth-planes]].

notes.title: Strings accompanying a soloist, and piano-to-strings transcription
aliases: cuerda como acompañamiento de un solista
notes.use_when: Writing a string accompaniment under a vocal or instrumental soloist (aria, song, concerto slow movement, film solo), or turning a piano accompaniment into string parts.
notes.summary: Pick one of five accompaniment templates (bass on the beat + off-beat chords; sustained harmony + violin ostinato; sustained harmony + legato violin arpeggios; cello rhythm + soft pizz.; tremolo chords over a low melody), keep it one or two dynamic steps under the soloist and out of the soloist's register, and build it from subelements with different rhythms. Piano chords become repeated or sustained string notes, broken figures become pizz. (light) or arco (sustained), and the bass goes to Vc with Cb pizz. for punctuation.

notes.title: Counterpoint and fugato in the string section
notes.use_when: Writing two or more independent lines for strings alone (fugato, canon, a theme against a countermelody, Baroque concerto-grosso style), or checking why a string-only polyphonic passage sounds muddy.
notes.summary: In strings-only counterpoint colour cannot separate the lines, so rank them (primary, secondary, tertiary) and separate them by register band and by rhythm, thinning the counterpoint around the main theme; dynamics help least. Fugal entries traditionally climb from the basses to Vln I, each entering with a rhythmically distinct, pickup-driven subject.

notes.title: String section chords, spacing and divisi (homophonic writing)
aliases: disposición de acordes en la cuerda
notes.use_when: Voicing chords, a chorale, a hymn-like progression or a pad for strings, choosing which section takes which chord tone, or deciding when to divide sections.
notes.summary: Space string chords like the harmonic series (wide at the bottom, close at the top) in the order Cb–Vc–Vla–Vln II–Vln I; pick the colour by distribution (violas/cellos divisi = dark, everything an octave or two up without basses = luminous, cellos + basses on the bass = intense). Divide Vln II, Vla and Vc for rich chords but keep Vln I undivided and reinforced; give the basses one well-placed note.

notes.title: Writing for the string section (roles, planes, melody)
notes.use_when: Writing any passage for the string section as a whole (string orchestra or the strings inside the orchestra), deciding which section carries the melody, or balancing melody, counterpoint and accompaniment inside the strings.
notes.summary: Treat the strings as five independent voices (Vln I, Vln II, Vla, Vc, Cb), label every line foreground, middleground or background, and give the foreground its instrument's best register first; balance by register and scoring before dynamics. Save the highest register of a theme for its climax, keep background figures out of the melody's register and in a contrasting rhythm.

notes.title: Accompanying a concerto soloist
notes.style_scope: universal (Classical to 20th-c. concerto; applies to any soloist over an orchestral bed)
notes.use_when: Writing an orchestra (or orchestral bed) under a solo instrument: concerto passages, a SWAM soloist over sampled strings, a featured solo in a film cue.
notes.summary: An orchestral soloist fuses with the orchestra far more easily than a piano, so separate them actively: dialogue (solo first, tutti answers), role swaps, colour contrast (no orchestral instruments of the soloist's kind while it plays), rhythmic independence, thin simple beds, and register distance. Drop the tutti to p at a solo entry, especially in the soloist's weak register.

notes.title: Choosing and doubling the melody instrument
notes.style_scope: universal (Piston 1955, Adler 2002; tonal orchestral and film)
notes.use_when: Choosing which instrument plays a melody, deciding whether and how to double it (unison, octave, partial), or handing a wide line between instruments.
notes.summary: Pick the instrument whose comfortable register holds the tune and whose character fits; leave expressive solos undoubled (pure colour). To raise a melody, octave doubling adds brightness with little colour change, unison doubling changes the colour and adds weight (keep it for tutti and special effects), and partial doubling marks key notes. Keep weight in the upper octave, balance octaves by register, and hand wide lines over with a one-note overlap.

notes.title: Accompanying a singer, vocal ensemble or choir
notes.use_when: Writing orchestra under a solo voice (aria, song, recitative), a vocal ensemble, or a choir; or checking vocal ranges and pitch support.
notes.summary: Singers find pitch by ear, so lead them to each entry and keep pitch references in the orchestra, choirs even more than soloists. Keep the texture thin where the voice is weak (its lowest 5th) and avoid long dense accompaniment; contrast the voice in colour, register and rhythm, double it with violins only at the climax. Choirs: double the parts (colla parte or key notes), write each part in its best register, and use an accompanying figure that supports without covering.

notes.title: Accompanied melody (melody, bass, filler)
notes.use_when: Orchestrating a tune with accompaniment (the most common texture), designing the accompaniment layer, or moving a melody from one instrument to another.
notes.summary: Split the music into melody, bass and filler and give each its own instruments. The melody sits about one dynamic level above a transparent accompaniment built from 2–4 subelements with their own rhythms and rests, in idiomatic figuration and usually a contrasting colour or articulation. Hand the melody over at phrase boundaries, with a shared note or a common instrument, and re-colour it when a phrase repeats.

notes.title: Combined textures (layered complex tutti)
notes.use_when: Writing a climactic or busy tutti in which several distinct things happen at once (a theme, a countermelody, running figuration, a pedal), or running two whole textures against each other.
notes.summary: Plan 3–4 elements before writing notes, e.g. a brass chorale melody, a woodwind countermelody in faster values, a string scale or figuration line and a held pedal bass. Give each its own family, register band, rhythmic level and dynamic, and make the primary element a theme the listener already knows. Two whole textures can run at once when colour, pitch level and rhythm (even meter) differ; one is foreground, the other lighter background.

notes.title: Complex texture, mosaic, tapestry and micropolyphony
notes.style_scope: universal (Stravinsky, Ligeti, film action and suspense)
notes.use_when: Building a busy layered texture (magic shimmer, action bed, suspense cloud, primeval or machine atmosphere), or a section where no single element is primary.
notes.summary: A complex texture is either several simple textures stacked (see the combined-textures note) or a tapestry/mosaic of many elements with none primary. Build it from a few elements, each with its own register band, colour or technique and rhythmic grid, introduce each motive alone before stacking, and contrast decay types. For a micropolyphonic cloud, copy one line across many divisi tracks with small onset offsets so it fuses.

notes.title: Fugal entries, canon and stretto across the orchestra
notes.style_scope: universal (Baroque to 20th c.; entry orders era-tagged)
notes.use_when: Scoring a fugato, fugal exposition, canon or stretto, or any passage where a subject enters several times and each entry must be heard.
notes.summary: Make every entry heard: separate entries by colour family and register, state the subject alone first with a recognisable rhythm, and let the entering voice lead (f, marcato) over continuing voices at mf/p. Each new entry adds a colour, a family or a dynamic level. Entry order depends on period and family; canonic layers enter one bar apart, each in one family, with the head of each entry reinforced; close with stretto.

notes.title: Contrapuntal texture in the orchestra
notes.style_scope: universal (Baroque to film; period entry orders tagged in the split note)
notes.use_when: Orchestrating two or more independent lines of similar importance (fugue, canon, combined themes, a theme against another theme), or a tutti built from a few melodic lines.
notes.summary: A contrapuntal texture is made only of melodic lines (usually 2–5), each carried by a block of instruments in unison and/or octaves. Rank the lines, give each its own composite colour, register band and rhythm profile, let dissonances between them stand, and keep a distribution table line → instruments → octave. Watch where doublings put each line in pitch, break routine pairings when that separates lines, and keep pads out.

notes.title: Doubling real parts (voice leading in orchestration, chorale tutti)
notes.style_scope: universal (tonal music; checks assume common-practice voice leading)
aliases: conducción de voces en la orquestación
notes.use_when: Turning a voice-led progression or chorale (3–4 real parts) into a full orchestral layout, or checking that the doublings in a generated score do not spoil its voice leading.
notes.summary: Score a progression by writing correct real parts first, one instrument each, then add unison and octave doublings. Never double the bass above where it mixes with the upper voices, never double a part below the bass, and do not double the voice just above the bass with the top part an octave higher. Melodic progression beats vertical chord rules. Massive chorale tutti: strings SATB with basses 8vb, trumpets on top, horns on the tune an octave lower, trombones and tuba low, upper woods on the upper strings, low reeds on the bass, piccolo in its lowest octave.

notes.title: Part writing and chorale textures
notes.style_scope: universal (tonal harmonic writing; period variants tagged)
notes.use_when: Scoring 3–5 voice harmonic writing (a chorale, a hymn-like passage, a brass or woodwind choir, a cadence) for orchestra.
notes.summary: Part writing is a few real parts (usually 3–4) of about equal standing; every other staff is a unison or octave doubling of one of them. Write the real parts with clean voice leading first, then give each a mixed-timbre group or a pure-colour choir; unison doublings add weight, octave doublings add colour but little weight. Keep the upper voices close and the bass gap wide, and let parts change number and instruments at cadences.

notes.title: Secondary melody and countermelody
notes.use_when: Adding a countermelody under or around a main tune, writing a horn/cello answer in the gaps of a melody, or balancing a three-element texture (melody, secondary melody, accompaniment).
notes.summary: Piston's type III has three elements: main melody, secondary melody (obbligato or an equal theme) and accompaniment. Make the two melodic lines differ in colour, contour and rhythm (move when the tune holds) and give the three elements different rhythms and dynamics. The secondary line sits about one level below the main one and never above it in level; the main tune can win while outnumbered thanks to a high register and having been heard first.

notes.title: Orchestral texture types (classifier)
notes.style_scope: universal (Piston's typology, applies to tonal orchestral and film music)
notes.use_when: Before orchestrating a section, to decide which texture recipe to apply; or when analysing a reference to say what each instrument is doing.
notes.summary: Classify every section into one of Piston's seven textures (unison, melody and accompaniment, secondary melody, part writing, counterpoint, chords, complex), list its few elements (A melody, B accompaniment…) and their plane (foreground, middleground, background), then load the recipe note. Octave doublings and parallel 3rds/6ths are one element, not new voices. Change the layout every few bars and the texture at form boundaries.

notes.title: Tutti and octave-unison layouts (weighting by octave)
notes.use_when: Laying out a tutti or multi-octave unison octave by octave, choosing between a massive and a brilliant tutti, or checking which octave dominates.
notes.summary: Weight a multi-octave line in the middle octaves (about five players each) with one flute on top and basses below. Unison doublings add tone-weight, octave doublings add brightness but little weight, and horns or trumpets at f outweigh several woodwinds. A massive tutti packs everyone into two adjacent octaves; a brilliant one covers four or five octaves with every family in every octave.

notes.title: Orchestral unison and tutti
notes.use_when: A request says "unison", "all together", "tutti", "full orchestra", "épico todos juntos", or a climax needs the whole orchestra.
notes.summary: A unison gives one line to several timbres (actual unison or spread in octaves, which the ear hears as one line); use only instruments whose good register holds the whole line. A tutti (partial or grand) spreads the orchestra over about four octaves, weighted in the middle; strings and woodwinds carry a fast line while brass and timpani sustain or punctuate. Reserve the grand tutti and each family's strongest register for the structural peak.

notes.title: Band ↔ orchestra transcription (string effects for band, band colours for orchestra)
notes.style_scope: band and orchestral transcription (Adler's models — Milhaud *Suite française*, Schoenberg Op.43a/b; 20th-c. American practice)
notes.use_when: Converting an orchestral cue to concert band or wind ensemble, or a band/wind piece to orchestra, including mapping band-only instruments (saxes, cornets, euphonium) and string effects.
notes.summary: Map by function, not by name, and keep the foreground/background planes and the composer's colour choices. Band → orchestra: no orchestral section equals the band's clarinet mass, so thin each wind part to one player, move sustained countermelodies to strings, keep the brass in reserve, and thin the accompaniments. Orchestra → band: pick the wind that best makes each string effect (pizz. → staccato brass + mallet, single-note tremolo → xylophone or piano tremolo) and never try to imitate cellos + basses.

notes.title: Concert band and wind ensemble (line-up, score order, march texture, band tutti)
notes.style_scope: band and wind-ensemble music (20th-c. American concert band and wind ensemble; marches)
notes.use_when: Writing or arranging for concert band, street/marching band or wind ensemble, building a band template in REAPER, or writing a march.
notes.summary: A band doubles each part with an unknown number of players (ten clarinets on a line), so parts must work at any size; a wind ensemble (Fennell, 1952) has one player per part, like an orchestra without strings. Cornets, saxophones and euphonium carry real melodies. The clarinet choir does the strings' job (general knowledge). March = melody in high reeds/trumpets, afterbeats in horns/alto saxes, bass on 1 and 3, cymbals + bass drum with the bass. Build tuttis by adding families one by one.

notes.title: Woodwind chords, chorales, pedals and sustained harmony
notes.style_scope: universal (Classical–Romantic pedal and sustained-harmony layouts era-tagged)
notes.use_when: Voicing a woodwind chord, chorale or pad (pairs, threes or single winds), choosing a bright or dark woodwind voicing, writing wind pedals and held harmony under active strings, or balancing woodwind chords against brass.
notes.summary: Lay pair chords out stacked (default; check the top note's register), interlocked (blend; check the weaker partner) or enclosed; share a unison between pairs only in tutti. Avoid close one-timbre-per-note chords; put the widest gap at the bottom and keep the upper winds close. Bright = flutes high on top, dark = a low top voice. Winds hold pedals and slow sustained lines under busy strings, broken at phrase seams; against forte brass, double the woodwinds and put them on top.

notes.title: Woodwinds with strings (accompaniment, alternation, antiphony, doubling strings)
notes.style_scope: universal (Classical to 20th c.; unison-doubling habits era-tagged)
notes.use_when: Combining woodwinds with strings: winds accompanying a string tune, passing a figure between the sections, call-and-response, moving from a wind passage to strings, or deciding how winds double string lines in soft passages and tutti.
notes.summary: Winds accompany a string tune with off-beat dyads or a passed-around arpeggio; alternate short phrases between sections, rotate a motive across ≥3 timbres at different octaves, then merge both sections at the cadence and alter the third repetition. Double strings at the octave by default (unison for colour or tutti weight), one wind per octave at p and a2 at f, reinforce only weak string voices discreetly, and remove doublers to make a diminuendo.

notes.title: Woodwind section writing (functions, melody, counterpoint, articulation)
notes.style_scope: universal (Classical to 20th c.; period-bound rules are era-tagged)
aliases: escritura para la sección de madera
notes.use_when: Deciding what the woodwind section does in a passage, or scoring a woodwind melody or woodwind counterpoint (solo vs a2, octave pairs, colour pairs, leitmotif colour, pulsing or mixed articulation).
notes.summary: Strings are the continuous, homogeneous base; woodwinds are heterogeneous and get one function at a time (solo, harmonic background, colour contrast, doubling). Keep solos single (same-instrument unison only in tutti or fugal entries), reinforce by octave pairs of changing colour rather than unison, choose unison pairs by blend (Fl+Ob round, Ob+Cl mysterious, Fl+Cl ≈ clarinet alone at 70–78, bassoon an octave below anything), and keep each motive's colour fixed.

notes.title: Expression and dynamics curves over a phrase (measured)
notes.use_when: Drawing the CC11 (expression) or CC1 (dynamics layer) curve of a melodic phrase, a sustained line or a section legato.
notes.summary: Professionals start the phrase already high (60–75 % of its peak), move the curve 100–200 ms before the note-on, reach the target in 100–250 ms, peak in the first half, and fall only 5–25 points at the end. Section dynamics (CSS/CSW CC1) sit around 60–65, rarely above 95.

notes.title: Guitar performance with Ample Guitar (classical L) — keyswitches, velocity, legato, tremolo
notes.style_scope: Ample Sound guitars (measured on Ample Guitar L, the classical nylon guitar)
notes.use_when: Turning a solved guitar part into MIDI for an Ample Sound guitar, or when the user says a guitar "no suena creíble", sounds too strong, or the tremolo sounds mechanical.
notes.summary: Ample picks its own string unless a String Force keyswitch (31–36 = 6th…1st string) precedes each note; legato needs its keyswitch plus overlapping notes on one string; classical playing lives in the soft velocity layer (hard layer starts between 64 and 72). Choose plugin settings per piece from the R7 table (fresh instance: Auto Mod on, Auto Legato on, Start Time 35 ms; what each does per the manual, which value suits which texture, and how sure we are); always one empty bar before the first note; keep arpeggios even and tempo ramps smooth. Shape dynamics inside each figure, per phrase and per pickup. Tremolo: automate release 230 ms + Start Time 30 ms + Auto Mod off (drop per re-pluck 16.5 → 3.9 dB) and draw mod-wheel vibrato on long notes; finger model still to validate against real recordings.
sources: Ample Sound manuals (Documents/Ample Sound/Manuals: Main Panel AGL, Settings and CPC)
user and guitarist feedback, Fantasía de San Juan

notes.title: Legato overlaps, slur velocity and attack offsets (measured)
notes.use_when: Writing slurred lines (overlap length, velocity of slurred notes) or deciding how early to start notes of slow-attack patches.
notes.summary: Professional overlaps have a median of about 35 ms (p10–p90 about 10–150 ms) on modelled instruments and 50–170 ms on CSS/CSW. Slur velocity follows note length and drops on long, expressive notes. Early starts for slow attacks belong to the library: CSS compensates with a track delay, not per note. Measure Albion before trusting fixed offsets.

notes.title: Library translation table (what each controller means in our libraries)
notes.style_scope: the user's libraries (Albion ONE, SWAM, Symphony Series, Darwin Percussion Ensemble)
notes.use_when: Before turning a performance idea (phrase shape, dynamics, slur, timing) into MIDI for one of the user's libraries, or when transferring numbers measured on another library.
notes.summary: Separate the player (phrase shape relative to its peak, timing, breaths: transferable) from the library (which CC, its dB response, what velocity means, legato delay: not transferable). This table gives each of our libraries' translation and marks every fact as measured, documented or assumed.
sources: SWAM Solo Woodwinds v3.8.0 user manual

notes.title: Programming modelled soloists (SWAM, Sample Modeling)
notes.use_when: Writing or fixing MIDI for SWAM (Audio Modeling) or Sample Modeling solo instruments.
notes.summary: Modelled soloists need a continuous CC11 (breath or bow): without it there is no sound. CC1 is vibrato depth and velocity on an overlapping note sets the portamento time. Use the user-validated set in user-taste R17. Measured references put vibrato at 25–35 % into a long note, and SM strings sit at a CC11 median of 48–59.
sources: SWAM Solo Woodwinds v3.8.0 user manual (Audio Modeling)

notes.title: Tutti balance by role (measured in full mock-ups)
notes.use_when: Setting the relative dynamics of all parts in a tutti, or of a soloist over a bed, through CC1, CC11 and velocity instead of faders.
notes.summary: In professional mock-ups the faders stay at 0 dB and the balance lives in the MIDI. The melody moves most and sits a little higher; pads and inner voices sit lower and flatter. A soloist over a soft bed plays far higher on its dynamics layer. CC11 is often a static per-track trim around 90, while CC1 performs. Loud melody instruments (trumpets) play lower CC1 than the horns under them; weak doublings (flutes) are pushed up.

notes.title: Timing and velocity humanization (measured)
notes.style_scope: orchestral mock-ups (for pop/rock groove see user-taste R6 and R14)
notes.use_when: Deciding how much timing and velocity variation an orchestral part needs, or checking whether a part sounds quantized.
notes.summary: Played-in professional parts sit around the grid with a median offset of about 0, but a p10–p90 spread of ±25–45 ms, and only 6–14 % of the notes land within 3 ms of the grid. Short-note velocity has a standard deviation of about 20–26, with a small strong-beat accent. Our earlier ±4–6 ms was far too tight.

notes.title: Compose or arrange a modern song (pop, rock, folk, metal, hip hop, ballad)
notes.use_when: The user asks for a song, beat, cover or arrangement in a modern popular style (the usual case in this project).
notes.summary: The user's taste rules first. Then use the books where they add craft: song form with real contrast, voice-led pads and strings, purposeful harmonic colour, doublings and orchestral layers on choruses.

notes.title: Compose an orchestral / film cue in REAPER
notes.use_when: The user asks for an original orchestral, cinematic, epic, trailer-like or "soundtrack" piece or section.
notes.summary: Eight stages: brief, harmonic plan, section map with tension curve, template tracks, the five elements written per section, orchestration and doubling, validation, then hand-over for listening. Each stage has one required note; open the others only when that stage needs them. Total is about 8–12 notes.

notes.title: Harmonize a melody or turn a progression into voiced parts
notes.use_when: The user gives a melody to harmonize, a chord progression to voice for instruments, a bass to realise, or asks for a chorale/pad/brass chord part.
notes.summary: Choose the harmony (melody → chords via cadence points first), then voice it in four real parts with correct spacing and voice leading, then adapt the voicing to the target instruments and check parallels and ranges.

notes.title: Orchestrate existing material (piano sketch, MIDI, song)
notes.use_when: The user has a piano sketch, a MIDI reduction, a lead sheet or an existing song section and wants it played by orchestra or by a larger ensemble.
notes.summary: Dump the source MIDI, analyse it into melody / bass / harmonic filler per section, choose a texture per section, assign families and doublings, write idiomatic parts per instrument, then check balance and ranges.

notes.title: Plan a piece in a given form (before writing notes)
notes.use_when: The user names a form (minuet, sonata, rondo, variations, fugue, waltz, march, chorale…) or asks for a piece whose structure must be decided before writing.
notes.summary: Choose the form note, fill its planning template (sections, bars, keys, material, cadence), check the phrase grammar, then turn the plan into REAPER regions and a per-bar harmony plan before writing any melody.

notes.title: The user's validated taste (overrides the books)
notes.use_when: Before writing any music for this user, in any style. Read it with every workflow.
notes.summary: The user is a sound engineer who judges by ear. Their validated preferences beat any book rule. Write idiomatic parts per instrument, make the MIDI expressive, mark sections with space and contrast, and get the real chart/reference before writing a cover.
sources: user feedback sessions Oct 2026 (Claude memory: music-arrangement-principles, beat-making-preferences)

notes.title: Validate generated MIDI before handing it to the user
notes.use_when: After writing or editing any MIDI part, before telling the user it is ready.
notes.summary: Check ranges against data/instruments.json (full = error, practical = warning), then idiom limits, voice leading in chorale-like textures, balance and dynamics at arrivals, CC smoothness, and the build response.
